subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Saltatory conduction in myelinated neurones speeds transmission because:
options: The action potential jumps between nodes of Ranvier where depolarisation occurs
The axon diameter is reduced by the myelin
Myelin increases the membrane's permeability to sodium
Myelin actively pumps sodium along the axon
questions.explain: Depolarisation only occurs at the gaps (nodes of Ranvier), so the impulse appears to jump from node to node, greatly increasing speed.

questions.q: On a cold day, the body conserves heat by:
options: Increased sweating
Relaxation of erector pili muscles
Vasodilation of skin arterioles
Vasoconstriction of skin arterioles, reducing blood flow to the surface
questions.explain: Vasoconstriction reduces blood flow near the skin surface, decreasing heat loss by radiation.

questions.q: In the sliding filament theory, muscle contraction shortens the sarcomere because:
options: The actin and myosin filaments themselves shorten
Myosin heads form cross-bridges and pull the actin filaments past the myosin toward the centre
Calcium ions are pumped out of the sarcoplasm
The H zone widens as filaments slide apart
questions.explain: Myosin heads bind actin and, powered by ATP, pull the thin filaments inward so the sarcomere shortens while filament lengths stay the same.

questions.q: When the water potential of the blood falls, ADH is released and causes:
options: More aquaporins to be inserted into the collecting duct, increasing water reabsorption
The loop of Henle to pump out more sodium
Less water to be reabsorbed, producing dilute urine
Increased filtration at the glomerulus
questions.explain: ADH makes the collecting duct walls more permeable by inserting aquaporins, so more water is reabsorbed and concentrated urine is produced.

questions.q: At a cholinergic synapse, the arrival of an action potential at the presynaptic membrane triggers:
options: Influx of potassium ions
Reuptake of acetylcholine
Direct flow of current across the cleft
Opening of voltage-gated calcium channels, causing vesicles to fuse and release acetylcholine
questions.explain: Depolarisation opens Ca2+ channels; calcium influx causes synaptic vesicles to fuse with the membrane and release neurotransmitter by exocytosis.

questions.q: Glucagon raises blood glucose principally by stimulating:
options: Insulin secretion from beta cells
Glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis in the liver
The conversion of glucose to fat
Glycogenesis and glucose uptake
questions.explain: Glucagon promotes breakdown of glycogen (glycogenolysis) and synthesis of glucose from non-carbohydrate sources (gluconeogenesis) in the liver.

questions.q: The resting potential of a neurone (about -70 mV) is maintained by:
options: Equal diffusion of sodium and potassium ions
Voltage-gated sodium channels being open
Continuous influx of sodium ions
The sodium-potassium pump (3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in) and the membrane's greater permeability to K+
questions.explain: The Na+/K+ pump plus relatively high K+ permeability (and large anions inside) make the inside negative relative to the outside.

questions.q: In the second messenger model of glucagon action, the binding of glucagon to its receptor leads to:
options: Activation of adenylate cyclase, raising cyclic AMP, which activates protein kinase A
Opening of voltage-gated sodium channels
Insulin being released by exocytosis
Direct entry of glucagon into the cell to activate enzymes
questions.explain: Glucagon activates adenylate cyclase, producing cAMP as a second messenger that activates protein kinase A to trigger glycogenolysis.

questions.q: Type 1 diabetes differs from type 2 in that:
options: Type 1 is caused by target cells losing responsiveness to insulin
Type 1 has a later onset and is linked to obesity
Type 1 is usually treated by diet and exercise alone
Type 1 results from autoimmune destruction of beta cells so little or no insulin is produced
questions.explain: In type 1 the immune system destroys insulin-secreting beta cells, whereas type 2 involves reduced insulin sensitivity of target cells.

questions.q: Ultrafiltration in the renal glomerulus occurs because:
options: Plasma proteins are actively secreted into the filtrate
High hydrostatic blood pressure forces small molecules through the basement membrane, which acts as a filter
The afferent arteriole is wider than the efferent arteriole, lowering pressure
Active transport pushes plasma into the Bowman's capsule
questions.explain: High pressure (helped by a narrower efferent arteriole) forces water and small solutes through the basement membrane, which holds back proteins and cells.

questions.q: Depolarisation during an action potential is caused by:
options: Chloride ions entering the axon
The sodium-potassium pump reversing direction
Voltage-gated sodium channels opening and Na+ flooding into the axon
Potassium ions diffusing out of the axon
questions.explain: At threshold, voltage-gated Na+ channels open and Na+ rushes in, making the inside positive (depolarisation).

questions.q: The repolarisation phase of an action potential is brought about by:
options: Potassium channels opening so K+ diffuses out of the axon
The sodium-potassium pump alone
Sodium channels opening
Calcium ions entering the axon
questions.explain: Voltage-gated K+ channels open and K+ leaves the axon, restoring the negative internal potential (repolarisation).
